items.title: Four More Dilemmas, Now Aimed at the Second Reason — Deliberate Action

items.zh: 若取比量義者，如愚稚等未能思度，不應率爾起於我覺。又我今問汝，隨汝意答。如世間所作，為以覺為因？為以我為因？若以覺為因者，執我所作，不應道理。若以我為因者，要先思覺，得有所作，不應道理。
items.en: If through inference, then even foolish children, incapable of reasoning, should not so readily arrive at a sense of self. Further, I now ask you, answer as you see fit: is worldly action caused by mere cognition, or caused by a self? If caused by mere cognition, then to insist it is caused by a self makes no sense. If caused by a self, then requiring a prior deliberate intention before any action can occur makes no sense.

items.zh: 又汝何所欲？所作事因常無常耶？若無常者，此所作因，體是變異；執我有作，不應道理。若是常者，即無變異；無變有作，不應道理。
items.en: Further, what do you actually intend: is the cause of action permanent, or impermanent? If impermanent, its own substance undergoes change, and to hold that a self acts makes no sense. If permanent, it undergoes no change at all — yet something utterly unchanging producing action makes no sense either.

items.zh: 又汝何所欲？為有動作之我能有所作？為無動作之我有所作耶？若有動作之我能有所作者，是即常作，不應復作。若無動作之我有所作者，無動作性，而有所作，不應道理。
items.en: Further, what do you actually intend: does a self with motion produce action, or a self without motion? If a self with motion produces action, it would then be acting perpetually, and should not need to act again — which makes no sense. If a self without motion produces action, then something with no capacity for motion at all nonetheless producing action makes no sense.

items.zh: 又汝何所欲？為有因故我有所作？為無因耶？若有因者，此我應由餘因策發方有所作，不應道理。若無因者，應一切時作一切事，不應道理。
items.en: Further, what do you actually intend: does the self act because of some further cause, or without any cause at all? If because of some further cause, then the self must first be roused to action by that further cause — which makes no sense. If without any cause at all, then it should be doing everything at all times — which makes no sense.

items.title: Does the Self Act on Its Own, or Depend on Something Else?

items.zh: 又汝何所欲？此我為依自故能有所作？為依他故能有所作？若依自者，此我自作老病死苦雜染等事，不應道理。若依他者，計我所作，不應道理。
items.en: Further, what do you actually intend: does this self act depending only on itself, or depending on something else? If depending only on itself, then this self would be bringing about its own ageing, sickness, death, suffering, and defilement — which makes no sense. If depending on something else, then claiming the self is what acts makes no sense.

items.title: Four Places a Self Might Hide Relative to the Aggregates — All Impossible

items.zh: 又我今問汝，隨汝意答。為即於蘊施設有我？為於諸蘊中？為蘊外餘處？為不屬蘊耶？若即於蘊施設我者，是我與蘊無有差別；而計有我諦實常住，不應道理。
items.en: Further, I now ask you, answer as you see fit: is the self posited as identical to the aggregates? Within the aggregates? Somewhere apart from the aggregates? Or unrelated to the aggregates entirely? If the self is posited as identical to the aggregates, then the self is no different from the aggregates — yet to claim the self is truly, permanently existing makes no sense.

items.zh: 若於諸蘊中者，此我為常？為無常耶？若是常者，常住之我為諸苦樂之所損益，不應道理。若無損益，起法非法，不應道理。若不生起法及非法，應諸蘊身、畢竟不起；又應不由功用，我常解脫。
items.en: If the self dwells within the aggregates, is it permanent, or impermanent? If permanent, then a permanent self being harmed or benefited by pain and pleasure makes no sense. If it is neither harmed nor benefited, then its ever giving rise to right or wrong conduct makes no sense. And if it gives rise to neither right nor wrong conduct, then the aggregate-body should never arise at all — and the self should already be permanently liberated without any effort whatsoever.

items.zh: 若無常者，離蘊體外，有生有滅相續流轉法不可得，故不應理。又於此滅壞，後於餘處不作而得，有大過失，故不應理。
items.en: If impermanent, then apart from the substance of the aggregates, no further phenomenon subject to arising, ceasing, and continuous flow can ever be found — this makes no sense. And to say that, once destroyed here, the self is then obtained elsewhere without any further action producing it, carries a grave fault — this makes no sense either.

items.zh: 若蘊外餘處者，汝所計我應是無為，不應道理。若不屬蘊者，我一切時應無染污，又我與身不應相屬，此不應理。
items.en: If the self exists somewhere apart from the aggregates, then the self you posit should be unconditioned — which makes no sense. If the self is unrelated to the aggregates entirely, then it should be forever undefiled at every moment, and the self should have no relationship whatsoever to this body — which makes no sense.

items.title: Is the "Seer" the Very Act of Seeing, or Something Apart From It?

items.zh: 又汝何所欲？所計之我，為即見者等相？為離見者等相？若即見者等相者，為即於見等假立見者等相？為離於見等別立見者等相？若即於見等假立見者等相者，則應見等是見者等；而汝立我為見者等，不應道理。以見者等與見等相無差別故。
items.en: Further, what do you actually intend: is the self you posit identical to the mark of "the seer" and the like, or apart from that mark? If identical to it, is that mark of "the seer" posited directly upon the act of seeing itself, or posited apart from that act? If it is posited directly upon the act of seeing itself, then the act of seeing simply is the seer — and your positing a self as the seer, distinct from the mere act, makes no sense, since the mark of "the seer" and the mark of "seeing" are then no different from each other at all.

items.title: Five Analogies for "Self as the Doer of Seeing" — All Fail

items.zh: 若離於見等別立見者等相者，彼見等法為是我所成業？為是我所執具？若是我所成業者，若如種子，應是無常，不應道理。若言如陶師等，假立丈夫。此我應是無常，應是假立；而汝言是常是實，不應道理。
items.en: If the seer is posited apart from the act of seeing itself, then is the act of seeing something the self produces as its own action, or an instrument the self merely wields? If it is the self's own produced action — comparable to a seed producing a sprout — then, like a seed, the self should be impermanent; yet you claim it is permanent, so this makes no sense. If you compare it instead to a potter, a conventionally designated agent, then this self should likewise be impermanent and merely conventionally designated; yet you claim it is permanent and truly real, so this makes no sense either.

items.zh: 若言如具神通，假立丈夫。此我亦應無常假立，於諸所作隨意自在。此亦如前，不應道理。若言如地，應是無常。又所計我，無如地大顯了作業，故不應理。何以故？世間地大所作業用，顯了可得。謂持萬物令不墜下，我無是業顯了可得。
items.en: If you compare it to a person endowed with supernormal powers, likewise conventionally designated, able to freely accomplish whatever is willed, this too, as before, makes no sense. If you compare it to the earth element, then, like earth, it should be impermanent. Further, the self you posit has no function as clearly evident as the earth element's — this makes no sense. The earth element's function in the world is plainly evident: it holds all things up, keeping them from falling. The self has no such plainly evident function.

items.zh: 若如虛空，應非實有。唯於色無假立空故，不應道理。虛空雖是假有，而有業用分明可得；非所計我，故不應理。世間虛空所作業用分明可得者，謂由虛空故，得起往來屈伸等業。是故見等是我所成業，不應道理。若是我所執具者，若言如鎌。如離鎌外，餘物亦有能斷作用；如是離見等外，於餘物上見等業用不可得故，不應道理。
items.en: If you compare it to empty space, then it should not be truly, substantially existent, since space is merely a name conventionally applied wherever matter is absent — this makes no sense. And though space is only conventionally existent, its function is nonetheless plainly evident, unlike the self you posit — this too makes no sense. Space's plainly evident function in the world is this: because of space, coming and going, bending and stretching, and every such motion becomes possible. It is therefore unreasonable to hold that seeing and the rest are the self's own produced action.

blocks.text: Today the treatise attacks the second reason for believing in a self: that action needs an agent. It then tests every relation a self could have to the aggregates, and every way a self could be "the seer" of seeing. Treat these arguments as guided contemplation; each one asks you to look for the self in a particular place and report what you find.

If deliberate action needs a self behind it, how does that self act? If the self moves, being permanent "it should act perpetually". Master Cháng Bǎi: "Cooking in the morning, one should go on cooking without stopping"; the eye "looks at plants and trees a while, then stops". Real activity starts and stops; a permanent agent could not.

subs.head: On its own, or depending on something else?

blocks.text: If the self acts by its own power, then, Master Cháng Bǎi asks, "why would it give itself ageing, sickness, death, and defilement?" Nobody chooses those. If it depends on something else, then the "something else" is the real cause, and the self adds nothing.

subs.head: Four places the self might be

blocks.text: The treatise tests four relations of a self to the aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness):

items: **Identical to the aggregates.** Then it is impermanent like them, contrary to the claim.

**Within the aggregates**, untouched by them. Then, the treatise says, the aggregate-body "should never arise at all, and the self should already be permanently liberated without any effort". Master Cháng Bǎi: then no one would need to practise.
**Somewhere apart from them.** Venerable Miào Jìng's image: "the aggregates are in San Francisco and the self is in New York". What would make it *this* person's self?
**Unrelated to them.** Then it "should be forever undefiled" and have no connection to this body.

blocks.text: Venerable Miào Jìng adds a distinction: the opponent calls the self "permanent" (a claim about time) and "real" (a claim about substance). Every option fails one test or the other.
This fourfold test is the classical Buddhist analysis. It is the same search Nāgārjuna uses with the chariot and its parts, and the same one meditators are taught to make with their own experience.

Is the self "the seer"? If "the seer" is just the act of seeing, then seeing simply is the seer, and positing a self adds nothing. If seeing is something the self produces, like a sprout from a seed, then the self is like a seed, and seeds are impermanent. Venerable Miào Jìng enjoys the image: "If the seed could talk, it would say, 'This sprout isn't me, but it's what I put out.'"

The opponent offers analogies: the self is to seeing as a cutter to cutting, as earth to what it supports, and so on. The treatise takes each in turn. Earth has a plain function, holding things up, which the self lacks; and earth is not permanent either. Venerable Miào Jìng: "mountains become seas and seas mountains."

The pattern of the whole argument is now clear. Every analogy that would explain a self's role turns out to describe an impermanent process that works perfectly well without a self. Tomorrow's reading draws this conclusion with fire, rivers, and lamps.

quiz.q: The text asks whether a self with motion acts — if so, it "should act perpetually." What everyday example does Master Cháng Bǎi give?
options: cooking breakfast, one should cook forever without stopping, since the self is unchanging; yet the eye looks at plants and then stops
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Cooking in the morning, one should go on cooking without stopping, since the self is permanent"; "the eye sees plants and trees, looks a while, then stops." Venerable Miào Jìng: in fact we act sometimes, stop, and act again — "acting again."

quiz.q: Does the self act depending on itself or on another? If on itself, why does it fail, according to Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: a self in charge would be foolish — why would it give itself ageing, sickness, death, and defilement?
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Then the self would be rather foolish — why would it give itself ageing, sickness, death, and defilement?" Venerable Miào Jìng: none of us wants to age, sicken, or die. If it depends on another, it isn't the self acting. The truth: "Everything arises from conditions; no self is in charge."

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what four relations between self and aggregates are tested?
options: identical to the aggregates, within them, elsewhere apart from them, unrelated to them
quiz.why: "Is the self posited as identical to the aggregates? Within the aggregates? Somewhere apart from the aggregates? Or unrelated to the aggregates entirely?" Venerable Miào Jìng: the first is "the aggregates are the self"; the other three are "a self apart from the aggregates." C is the tetralemma form of §40.

quiz.q: If a permanent self dwells in the aggregates, untouched and giving rise to neither right nor wrong conduct, what absurd result follows? How do the teachers put it?
options: the aggregate-body would never arise and the self would be liberated without effort — then no one would need to practise or ordain
quiz.why: "The aggregate-body should never arise at all — and the self should already be permanently liberated without any effort whatsoever." Master Cháng Bǎi: "Then the self would always be liberated without practice — why is it still suffering and enjoying?" Venerable Miào Jìng: "Then there'd be no need for the holy life, no great hardship, no ordaining against one's parents' wishes."

quiz.q: If the mark of "the seer" is posited directly on the act of seeing, what fault follows?
options: seeing simply is the seer; the two marks don't differ, so positing a self as seer makes no sense
quiz.why: "Then the act of seeing simply is the seer — and your positing a self as the seer … makes no sense, since the mark of 'the seer' and the mark of 'seeing' are then no different." Master Cháng Bǎi cites a verse from the Stage of Reflection: conditioned dharmas arise and cease instantly; when they function, they are provisionally called agents. Venerable Miào Jìng: "The seer is just the seeing; to call a self the seer is wrong."

quiz.q: If seeing is the self's produced action, like a seed producing a sprout, how does Venerable Miào Jìng put the analogy?
options: if the seed could talk it would say, "This sprout isn't me, but it's my output" — yet seeds are impermanent, so the self would be too
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "If the seed could talk, it would say, 'This sprout isn't me, but it's what I put out.'" The text: "like a seed, the self should be impermanent." Master Cháng Bǎi: a seed that sprouts is impermanent, so the self would be too. The potter and the person with powers are likewise designated and impermanent.
